segments.text: Math is the magic that powers AI, but you ask AI questions in words, not numbers.
And mathematically driven systems still have to process them.
This interface shows exactly what that looks like.
You ask a question in words, and the answer comes back in words.
You ask, what's the best Avengers movie?
AI answers.
Most people point to Avengers Endgame.
It's the big payoff to a decade of films, and it broke box office records.
Infinity War is the other top pick if you like a darker ending.
So how do your words become numbers?
One obvious idea is to assign every single word in a language its own unique
permanent number.
You type the word, the AI gets the number.
But that system breaks down almost instantly.
People constantly invent new slang, make typos, and
throw in things like emojis or lines of code.
Even if you built a dictionary with a million numbered words,
it wouldn't cover everything a human might type.
Instead of giving every word its own number,
AI uses reusable pieces of text called tokens.
This graphic shows how those tokens act as the building blocks for language.
The model's full collection of these building blocks is called its vocabulary.
Watch how a single complex word is broken down.
The text unbelievable goes in, and three specific chunks come out.
Un, Belie, and Vable.
One word is built from three pieces.
Notice that the letters following the prefix un are split into multiple tokens.
This system is incredibly efficient.
The same piece shows up in different words.
The chunk un starts unbelievable, unmatchable, and unusual.
The vocabulary simply reuses that piece instead of storing a separate entry for
every single word that starts with it.
That is the primary rule of the system, reuse the pieces, build more words.
When setting up an AI, engineers choose exactly how text will be split,
and a program analyzes massive amounts of text to build that vocabulary.
These collections are large.
Chat GPT holds about 200,000 tokens, Gemini about 256,000, and
Anthropic hasn't published Clods.
Each token is then assigned a number, its token ID.
Think of it as an address that identifies the token, but
says nothing about its actual meaning.
This flowchart breaks down what happens chronologically when you send a prompt.
Step one, you start with text by typing a question or message.
Step two, a program called a tokenizer breaks that text into reusable chunks.
In step three, the tokenizer looks up the IDs.
Using the claw 100k base tokenizer in this example,
it finds the specific numeric ID for each chunk.
For the word unbelievable, un gets 359, belee gets 32898, and
vable gets 24694.
Tokenization turns text into token IDs the model can use.
This image contrasts the human experience of language with the AIs.
Humans see a cat, and you have instant understanding.
You know what it means, fur whiskers the animal.
But for AI, the tokenizer simply converts to
the written word cat to ID 4719.
The number is just a structural tag.
A token ID identifies the token, meaning comes later.
This list shows how AI chops up text.
In example two, basketball becomes two tokens, basket and ball.
Example four covers spacing and symbols.
I heart AI splits into I, then a space with a heart, then a space with AI.
Notice that SP marks a leading space.
That shows how space is attached to the chunk that follows them,
resulting in three tokens total.
Finally, complex nonstandard text.
The web address shown on the board in example five breaks into eight strange chunks.
If the AI operates entirely in these numerical IDs,
how does the final answer become words again?
The mathematical process simply runs in reverse.
When the AI generates a reply, it outputs those IDs.
The tokenizer converts the IDs back into pieces of text and
snaps them together to form the readable answer you see on your screen.
This graphic sums it up perfectly, words become numbers.
That lets AI work with your language using math.
